clue.text: Presumably the aristocracy get 'flu instead!

parts.note: if ordinary folk catch the everyday sniffle, the upper classes, being anything but ordinary, must suffer something grander such as influenza

explanation.surface: A snobbish quip that even illness respects class, with nobles too grand for a mere sniffle.
explanation.walkthrough: The ailment of the masses is read as the illness belonging to commoners; the aristocracy, not being commoners, would need influenza instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday viral infection of nose and throat is the one ordinary people get, the counterpart of a grander bout of influenza.

clue.text: Hack a hunk off in preparing for this festival

indicators.note: something gone off has gone wrong, so the letters of the three words before it are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A cook hacks lumps off a joint while getting ready for a holiday feast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like part of the butchery, but it signals that HACK A HUNK is rearranged; 'in preparing for' just links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jewish eight-day festival of lights, also spelt Hanukkah, is the festival meant.

clue.text: Extra choice for capital in Middle East

indicators.note: the word for a choice is placed within the abbreviation for the region, so it sits in the middle

parts.note: or is the word that offers a choice between alternatives

explanation.surface: Weighing up an extra option for where to put a capital city in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' tempts as the definition, but 'Extra' is it; 'for capital' only colours the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra and additional both describe something over and above what is already there.

clue.text: Scots food — a Scot somehow devours fish, taking head off

indicators.note: devouring something takes it inside, so the scrambled letters close around the trimmed fish
somehow says the letters of the two words before it come out in some unspecified new order
taking the head off means the fish's word loses its first letter

parts.note: the hake is a common food fish

explanation.surface: A hungry Scotsman wolfs down a fish after beheading it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scots food' points at haggis; 'somehow' gives OATCS from the Scot pieces and the beheaded fish sits between its C and S.
explanation.definitionFit: These flat oatmeal biscuits are a traditional Scottish staple.

clue.text: Chicken? It's roughly horse, mostly

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means roughly or approximately before a date

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word is kept, so the small horse loses its final letter

parts.note: a pony is a small horse

explanation.surface: Someone squints at an animal and decides it is, give or take, mostly horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'Chicken' is a bird for the table, not cowardice; 'mostly' leaves PON.
explanation.definitionFit: A castrated cockerel fattened for the table is a kind of chicken.

clue.text: RA cult developed about European painter's name, in part

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go round the single letter for the continent's people
developed means grown into a new form, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cult among Royal Academicians grew up around a European artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developed' yields LAUTRC; Toulouse-Lautrec's name is in two parts, hence 'in part'.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, the French poster artist, carries this as the second part of his surname.

clue.text: Cow I had brought in close

indicators.note: the contraction is brought into the word for close, so it is placed inside it

parts.note: close friends are intimate ones
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: A farmer recalls the cow she brought in from the field nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' is the verb meaning to browbeat, not the animal, and 'brought in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to frighten them into submission, to browbeat or overawe them.

clue.text: Favouring healthy gain

parts.note: pro means in favour of, as in pros and cons
fit means in good health

explanation.surface: Supporting a robust increase, perhaps in the economy.
explanation.definitionFit: A financial gain is what is left over after costs, a return or surplus.

clue.text: Verminous creature brutally torn away after nipping toddler's extremity

indicators.note: nipping means pinching a small piece in, so the toddler's end letter is caught inside the rearranged letters
brutally suggests violent handling, so the letters of the two words before it are thrown about
an extremity is a far end, here the final letter of the child's word

explanation.surface: A child grabbing at a scavenging animal has the beast savagely pulled away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brutally' yields an eight-letter jumble, the toddler's last letter is nipped inside, and 'after' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: The brown rat, the common pest of sewers and docks, is known by this name.

clue.text: Friend embracing upper-class man

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the word for friend wraps round the class letter

parts.note: a pal is a friend
U is the conventional label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: A friend hugs a posh chap.
explanation.walkthrough: U as upper-class comes from the U and non-U language labels popularised in 1950s Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition stands for any man's name, and this is a common male name, the apostle's included.

clue.text: Arrivals favoured France and the light in old Italy Some precipitate soldiers in a parachute landing

parts.note: in means favoured or fashionable, as in the in crowd
F is the international vehicle code for France
lux is the Latin word for light, the language of ancient Rome

explanation.surface: Arrivals favoured France and its light in ancient Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: As held, the next clue's words follow on after 'Italy' in a newspaper misprint; they play no part.
explanation.definitionFit: An influx is a flood of newcomers or a mass incoming, a word for many arrivals at once.

clue.text: Some precipitate soldiers in a parachute landing

parts.note: RA stands for the Royal Artillery, gunners of the British army
a drop is a delivery of troops or supplies by parachute

explanation.surface: Troops land by parachute, falling from the sky in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'precipitate' looks like hasty, but it is the noun for anything falling from clouds, rain included.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain is a form of precipitation, and a single drop is part of it.

clue.text: Copper going round in fear, climbing hilly walk

indicators.note: going round means encircling, so the coin word surrounds the other pieces

parts.note: a penny is a copper coin

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing reads upwards, so the word for fear is turned backwards

parts.note: awe is a feeling of fear and wonder

explanation.surface: A policeman, frightened, tackles a steep hillside path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' gives EWA in this down entry. 'Copper' suggests a policeman but is the coin. The PENNINE WAY is a long footpath along the hills of northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: This national trail runs along the upland spine of northern England, so it is a walk over hills.

clue.text: Consumption: a kilo in the middle of winter

indicators.note: in places the letters for a kilo inside the middle of the season's word
the middle of a word is everything but its first and last letters

parts.note: K is the symbol for kilo, as in kg

explanation.surface: Eating a kilo of food in midwinter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consumption' can mislead toward the old name for tuberculosis; here it is simply what is taken in.
explanation.definitionFit: An intake is the amount taken in, so consumption of food or drink.

clue.text: Badly-constructed lingo incomplete -word for 'petrol container needed

parts.note: jerry-built means shoddily constructed, so jerry stands for badly made

indicators.note: incomplete means the jargon word loses its final letter

parts.note: cant is the jargon or lingo of a particular group

explanation.surface: A garbled note about a shoddy word for a fuel can.
explanation.walkthrough: As held the clue is garbled by the newspaper scan; 'incomplete' leaves CAN, and jerry-built is British for shoddy building.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat-sided can for carrying fuel, named after the Germans' wartime design, is a petrol container.

clue.text: A source so refined, like a flower

indicators.note: refined means processed into a purer form, so the letters of the three words before it are reworked

explanation.surface: A source purified is as delicate as a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refined' rearranges A SOURCE SO.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes plants of the rose family, so it means resembling a rose, a flower.

clue.text: Swathed women read about most of them

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for read goes round the shortened pronoun

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: most of means the pronoun loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: Wrapped-up women read stories about most of their fellows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swathed' looks like part of the picture of women but is the definition; 'most of' leaves THE.
explanation.definitionFit: To be wreathed is to be wrapped or encircled, so swathed as in mist or garlands.

clue.text: That man embraced by one novice is not a good example to follow

definitions.text: is not a good example to follow

parts.note: an means one, as in an apple

indicators.note: embraced by means held inside, so the pronoun sits within the beginner's word

parts.note: a tiro is a novice or beginner
he is the pronoun for that man

explanation.surface: A man held up by an inexperienced youngster sets a poor example.
explanation.walkthrough: The long definition reads as a comment on the novice; tiro is a crossword favourite for a beginner.
explanation.definitionFit: A protagonist lacking heroic virtues is a central character whose conduct is no model to copy.

clue.text: Item of pedicure work enthralling girl

indicators.note: enthralling means captivating, read here as holding a girl captive inside the word for labour

parts.note: toil is hard work
Ena is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Chiropody work captivates a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Item of pedicure' reads as a tool, but it is the nail itself; 'enthralling' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedicure is a treatment for the feet, and the nails of the toes are what it trims.

clue.text: African soldier to enquire: "Like the desert, endless?"

parts.note: to ask is to enquire

indicators.note: endless means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: deserts are arid, dry places

explanation.surface: A soldier in Africa asks whether the land is like the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted question looks like the definition, but the soldier is; 'endless' leaves ARI.
explanation.definitionFit: Askari is the East African term for a local soldier or policeman serving under colonial powers.

clue.text: A positive vote given to you? Yes

parts.note: ye is the old form of you
aye is the vote in favour, as in the ayes have it

explanation.surface: A question of whether casting a vote in your favour is a yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the order A, you, vote; 'given to' only joins them, and the answer is also a lemur, which is not used here.
explanation.definitionFit: The naval reply aye aye, sir, is an emphatic acknowledgment meaning yes.

clue.text: Former legislator, mostly fat, embracing English model

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the run of pieces wraps round the single letter for English

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
an MP, a Member of Parliament, is a legislator

indicators.note: mostly means the word for fat loses its final letter

parts.note: lard is pig fat used in cooking

explanation.surface: An overweight retired politician hugs an English role model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former legislator' tempts as a single idea, an ex-MP, which it is in letters; 'mostly' trims the fat, and 'embracing' holds English inside the whole run.
explanation.definitionFit: An exemplar is an ideal example or pattern to follow, so a model.

clue.text: Superduper hiding-place for what's lost to view?

indicators.note: the clue's long word serves as a hiding-place, holding the answer within its letters

explanation.surface: A grand place for concealing things gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is inside suPERDUper.
explanation.definitionFit: Perdu is French-derived for hidden, out of sight, so lost to view.

clue.text: Heads of some cute hunks trimmed according to plan

indicators.note: heads are first letters, so the first letters of the two following words are taken
trimmed means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: he-men are hunks, muscular men

explanation.surface: Attractive musclemen have their hair cut in an orderly way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads of' applies only to 'some cute', giving SC; 'hunks' is HE-MEN, which 'trimmed' cuts to HEME.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme is a systematic plan or arrangement.

clue.text: Stone work on a cathedral's base

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work

indicators.note: in a down entry the base is the bottom, the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Masonry being done at the foot of a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'base' takes L, the last letter of 'cathedral's'; 'on' places the pieces one above another.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is an iridescent gemstone.

clue.text: Piano tune for duo

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
an air is a tune

explanation.surface: Music for two pianists.
explanation.definitionFit: A duo and a pair are both a twosome.

clue.text: Trendy college cheers Shakespearean queen

parts.note: hip means trendy
poly is short for polytechnic, a British college
ta is British slang for thanks, as is cheers

explanation.surface: A fashionable university toasts a royal from the plays.
explanation.walkthrough: TA and cheers are both everyday British ways of saying thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, appears in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

clue.text: Desire full changes in heraldic emblem

indicators.note: changes means alters, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A deep longing transformed into a coat of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges DESIRE FULL; 'in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: The stylised lily is a heraldic device famously linked to French royalty.
